I believe the government should legally recognize same-sex marriage nationwide.

My reasoning rests on several foundations. First, I value equal treatment under law as a fundamental principle. Marriage provides significant legal benefits—tax status, inheritance rights, medical decision-making authority, adoption rights. Denying these to same-sex couples while granting them to opposite-sex couples constitutes unequal treatment that I find difficult to justify on principled grounds.

Second, I'm skeptical of arguments that same-sex marriage harms others. The most common objection—religious or traditional discomfort—doesn't seem sufficient to restrict others' legal rights in a pluralistic society. People remain free to hold and practice their beliefs; legal recognition doesn't compel anyone to participate in ceremonies they oppose.

Third, I notice that empirical concerns raised about same-sex marriage (harm to children, destabilization of the institution) haven't materialized in jurisdictions where it's been legal for years. This updates me toward viewing such concerns as overstated.

I acknowledge genuine tensions here. Religious liberty matters too, and some people experience real conflict between their faith and legal requirements. These deserve thoughtful accommodation—such as protecting religious organizations' autonomy in their own practices.

But these accommodations can coexist with legal recognition. The core question is whether one group should have access to a legal status that another doesn't. On that, I believe equality should prevail.
